title: Interfaces
subtitle: Define object shapes with interface — required, optional, readonly
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: JavaScript objects can have any shape — there's no enforcement that a 'user' object has a name, email, and age. Functions that expect a user object have no way to communicate what properties they need.
whyItExists.solution: An interface defines the required shape of an object. Any object with those properties (and types) satisfies the interface. TypeScript enforces this at every use site.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Anytime you're typing an object: API response shapes, function parameters that take objects, config objects, class contracts.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Interfaces can't represent union types or computed types easily — use type aliases for those. For simple one-off objects in a function, inline typing is fine.

explainModes.beginner: An interface is a blueprint for an object. You say 'any User must have a name (string), an email (string), and an age (number)'. Then TypeScript checks every place you create or use a User — if a property is missing or the wrong type, it's an error.
explainModes.simple: interface Name { prop: Type; }. Optional property: prop?: Type. Readonly: readonly prop: Type. Extending: interface B extends A { ... }. Implementing in class: class C implements I { ... }. Index signatures: [key: string]: number — any string key maps to number. Method signature in interface: greet(name: string): void.
explainModes.standard: TypeScript uses structural typing — if an object has all the properties an interface requires, it satisfies the interface, even if it has extra properties (excess property check only happens on literal object assignments). Interface merging (declaration merging): two interface declarations with the same name are merged — useful for extending third-party types. Interfaces can extend multiple interfaces: interface C extends A, B.
explainModes.technical: Interface vs type alias: interfaces are open (can be merged, extended by other interfaces), type aliases are closed. Both support extends-like behavior (type T = A & B for type, interface I extends A for interface). Prefer interfaces for object shapes that might be extended; prefer type aliases for unions, intersections, and computed types. Function interfaces: interface Fn { (x: number): number } — describes a callable. Hybrid types: interface Counter { (n: number): number; reset(): void } — callable AND has methods.
explainModes.deepDive: Declaration merging: adding properties to window or express.Request by declaring an interface with the same name. E.g., declare global { interface Window { myLib: typeof myLib } } — augments the Window interface. Module augmentation: import 'express'; declare module 'express' { interface Request { user?: User } } — adds user to req in Express. This is how @types packages add types to existing JS libraries without modifying them.

questions.question: What does `prop?: string` mean in an interface?
options: prop is required and must be a string or undefined
prop is optional — it may or may not be present on the object
prop can only be set once
questions.explanation: The ? makes a property optional — the object is valid whether or not it includes that property. TypeScript types optional properties as string | undefined when accessed. Without ?, the property is required and TypeScript errors if it's missing.

faq.q: What's the difference between interface and type alias?
faq.a: For object shapes, they're mostly equivalent. Key differences: interfaces can be extended with extends and support declaration merging (two declarations with same name merge); type aliases support union types (A | B), intersection types (A & B), and mapped types. Rule of thumb: use interface for objects and class contracts, type for unions and complex type expressions.

examples: interface ApiResponse<T> { data: T; status: number; message: string }
interface ButtonProps { label: string; onClick(): void; disabled?: boolean }
interface Repository<T> { findById(id: number): Promise<T>; save(entity: T): Promise<void> }
